ok so let me explain why subagents kill long context
Like you can spend $500m building 100 million context models, and they would be 1) slow, 2) expensive to use, 3) have huge context rot. O(n) is the lower bound.
Cog's approach is something you learn in day 1 of @CS50 - divide and parallelize. Embeddings are too dumb, Agentic Search is too slow. So train limited-agency (max 4 turns), natively parallel tool calling (avg parallelism of 7-8, custom toolset) fast (2800tok/s) subagents to give the performance of Agentic Search under an acceptable "Flow Window" that feels immaterially slower than Embeddings.
The benefit of this is threefold:
- 8 ^ 4 toolcalls cover a very large code search space. can compound subagent calls if more needed.
- predictable cost & end to end latency
- subagent outputs "clean" contexts, free of context failure modes like context poisoning and context rot (h/t @dbreunig )
we originally called this Rapid Agentic Search, to contrast with RAG. but Fast Context rolls of the tongue better.

mcps are changing
turns out designing mcps to load every tool definition into the model prompt was a bad idea
anthropic’s nov 4 blog post suggests a new pattern
treat each mcp server like a normal code library, e.g. typescript modules or files, and let the agent write and run small programs that do two things:
discover only what is needed, list a servers directory to see what exists, open just the specific tool files, import only those functions
process data locally, call mcp tools from code, then filter, join, and aggregate inside a sandboxed runner so only the small final bits go back to the model
doing this dramatically cuts tokens
anthropic shows a typical case dropping from 150k tokens down to ~2k (98.7% savings)

summary:
just discovered this exists, and not knowing about it was the main thing stopping me from building b2c llm wrappers
if you're an indie or solo developer and you hate dealing with users pasting api keys or having to manage llm billing and quotas inside your product, take a look at the claude agent sdk
if you build an app using the claude agent sdk, the user can simply sign in with their anthropic free, pro, or plus subscriptions, and their api usage will be deducted from their own quotas using anthropic oauth 2.0.
the claude agent sdk is somewhat model-agnostic, so you aren't strictly limited to claude as a model. but if you want to offer the option to select other models, you would have to deal with the problems mentioned before
sadly, openai and google still don't support user-level quota delegation, so anthropic + agent sdk is the only option for this right now (afaik)
this doesn't apply only to cli apps. you can also build ios apps and web apps that run llms in the backend via the agent sdk. the sign-on experience looks similar to google sign-in

title: alex fazio (@alxfazio)
summary:
i’m seeing a lot of confusion about skills in the comments
skills aren’t an mcp replacement in the strict sense. mcp is a protocol for connecting to external systems (largely, at least this is what they are used for), and skills are a way to package workflows, guidance, and runnable scripts. and yes, those scripts can call out to external systems too, even integrating mcp elements when needed
skills are designed for progressive disclosure by default. claude only pulls in the parts of a skill it needs when it needs them like instructions, scripts, or references and scripts or tool calls can run without dumping their entire contents into the context window. that alone fixes 99% of the problems that mcps have
it’s not that mcp is bad. it’s that mcp gets used like shit, because they don’t enforce best context engineering practices by design, when skills do. most mcp setups today just load a massive pile of tool definitions into context upfront.
sure, you can hack mcp to handle progressive disclosure too using filesystem or search based loading, state persistence, or code execution modes that cut token use by up to 98.7 percent but it’s not automatic. if the developer doesn’t build the mcp or client setup to dodge the schema dump, it will choke the context, because that’s the lazy default pattern
yes, you can build mcp setups that act more like the second approach, and anthropic has talked recently about modernizing the way mcp tool definitions get surfaced, like through code execution with sandboxes, so you don’t pay the “everything upfront” tax. great. but the point is with mcp, context-efficiency is something you have to fight for with extra work, and most implementations don’t bother. with skills, it’s basically the default setup, and they are way more flexible and easier to setup
so, mcp is valuable when you need standardized connectivity, authentication, and a reusable integration layer across many tools. but for the common “call an api and format the result” case, a skill plus scripts can be simpler and more context-efficient
mcps are more mature security-wise (atm), as they can be stricter with tool use and connection protocols, but if you care about security and correctness, you can still enforce guardrails with skills hooks, constrained tool usage patterns like allowed-tools, strict wrappers without making the model carry around a giant schema buffet just to order one sandwich
in the real world, a lot of mcp servers are basically api wrappers, because their nature is mostly that of connectors, whilst skills can do that and more. those same api requests can often get handled by a small, explicit script inside a skill yes, even something as stupid-simple as curl when that’s all you need, or more complex ones with packages like pypdf without dragging the entire mcp tool definition into the model context. and skills go way further than “call a function”: they can bundle custom scripts that run on demand, so you’re not stuck with a fixed rpc-style surface area.
mcps often just do exactly what the skill does, but with an additional unnecessary layer of abstraction:
mcp -> grab the appropriate tool definition -> tool call -> code execution
skill -> finds script with progressive disclosure -> code execution
^ here i’m largely summarising what actually goes into an mcp, which can be much more complex often unnecessarily
they’re supposed to be complementary, but i still think skills are going to win because they address the biggest practical pain point people experience with MCPs -> context rot, and allow for infinite flexibility in use

title: alex fazio (@alxfazio)
summary:
automation is great at producing output. but a lot of roles exist to carry responsibility, not just to produce artifacts or execute. until an ai can actually bear consequences or meaningfully change its behavior based on real world outcomes (stakes), it can’t fully replace the jobs built around being accountable
why can’t we just automate project managers, for example? it seems easy, right?
i’ve got some stream of consciousness thoughts on this, so take them with a grain of salt
i think the answer is accountability. a lot of jobs survive automation not because they’re critical (or complex), but because someone real has to be on the hook when things go sideways
like, imagine you automate a pm. the ai posts timelines, pings people, asks for updates… and the devs just ignore it. tbf, they’ll feel even more comfortable ignoring it because "it’s just another clanker". it doesn’t have a presence, it can’t read the room, and there’s no social cost to blowing it off. then what? on the management side, there’s no actual person to escalate, push back, or take heat when the project slips. management doesn’t want to (and often can’t) directly manage the execution layer, because at that point they’d have to become the project manager themselves
the ai can’t feel consequences the way a pm can. it has no skin in the game. getting fired, getting embarrassed in a meeting, losing political capital, taking a reputational hit, none of that registers in a way that changes what it does. so how is management supposed to raise the stakes to make the ai push the execution layer harder or get better at it? they can’t. they would have to be ai engineers (they aren't)
this dynamic is even stronger in bigger companies, where there are more layers and the accountability chain has more middlemen
execution jobs (like dev work) are easier to replace because they sit closer to the “do the thing” layer. the accountability from above is several steps removed from that layer
if a dev task doesn’t get done, the person who really has to answer for it to the boss usually isn’t the dev. it’s the pm, the em, the middle manager. they’re the ones who get dragged into the “why didn’t this ship?” conversation
in a smaller company with fewer layers, it’s a bit different. that separation can shrink a lot, sometimes the person doing the work is also the person answering for it. so the “replace the execution layer first” idea doesn’t map as cleanly. but that also means automation can be easier in a smaller company, and it can make more sense to spread the workload across agents

title: alex fazio (@alxfazio)
summary:
i'm building a fleet of vertical agents where each one gets its own full computer (100gb persistent disk, 8gb ram, ~600ms wake from hibernation) using sprites and glm 4.7. they're built entirely on claude code cli, no openclaw and no claude agent sdk. `claude --print` (non-interactive mode) is what makes this possible. the hatcher sends a prompt, claude code runs headlessly on the sprite, and streams structured json back. you can talk to them from discord or drop into a terminal and pick up the same session from anywhere
we call them droids. sprites give them ~$0 compute when idle and auto-hibernate after 30 seconds of inactivity. when a user sends a message, the sprite wakes in ~600ms and picks up right where it left off. they'll be hatchable from a base config using what i call a "droid hatcher," similar to botfather on telegram
we were already building useful vertical agents with claude code, but we're all busy and travel a lot. having to sit down in front of a laptop and open a terminal just to use claude code (because the app and don't have the same toolset) was creating a lot of friction. creating a new agent was an entire project. sharing one meant pushing to github, sharing the repo, pulling updates. group chats with claude code didn't exist, you couldn't have multiple people talking to the same agent in isolated threads. with this setup anyone in the company can hatch a new droid directly from discord using the droid hatcher, share it with others, or co-work on one together, all in full safety
i wanted something like openclaw for my business, but openclaw is too opinionated. it abstracts away too much of the claude code configuration, which kills customisation and portability. it would also force me to rewrite the claude code setups we already share across employees. and the agent sdk is too high-level for what i need. i want each droid to own its entire machine, not run inside someone else's runtime. because these are full claude code instances on isolated vms, the agents can self-improve, self-edit their own and their machines are fully auditable. we can ssh in and inspect anything at any time
this system solves all three problems. each droid is its own machine (no git pull needed), lives in a discord forum channel where each post is an independent session, and multiple people can interact with it concurrently
i can already resume a droid's session from a terminal whenever i want, instead of going through discord. their main home will be a dedicated discord server. i chose discord because i used midjourney a lot and i know what's possible on discord in terms of ux for bot-driven workflows. it also avoids dumping noise into our main slack channel, but they'll still be mentionable from slack when needed
anyone in my company will be able to create and customise their agent, all from a single chat. new people, collaborators, and contractors can be onboarded safely in discord, since each droid lives in its own forum channel and permissions are managed directly through discord roles. no complex business logic needed. contractors can even bring their own api key and hand it to the droid hatcher to spawn a droid they pay for, while still working transparently inside our org
the system supports third-party model providers like for tasks that don't need frontier intelligence. glm 4.7 is fast and cheap enough for most vertical agents. this also matters because anthropic has been banning accounts that use their max subscription inside third-party wrappers, and running through a separate api provider means your anthropic account stays clean
i think this is a better and safer version of both claude cowork and openclaw. each droid has its own isolated vm. not a shared sandbox, not a container, a full machine. if something goes wrong, you restore the entire machine from a previous checkpoint. no need to buy a mac mini just to feel safe, and no risk of an agent messing with your actual computer
this is probably the most fun llm project i've worked on so far. right now i only have a working slack prototype, but the signs are all there, and it has me genuinely excited. the full system with discord forum channels, the droid hatcher, and session forking is what's coming next. i already have a full design spec for the discord system and i'll share it when the time is right. i'll keep posting updates as it takes shape

turns out claude agent sdk is actually the better path over raw cc cli (claude -p) for my discord project
the cli works fine for multi-turn conversations, `--resume` and `--input-format stream-json` handle that. the limits show up when you need to interact with claude mid-turn. AskUserQuestion silently fails in headless mode (returns empty answers, no error). tool approval is static flags only, no runtime callback. skills don't load in `-p` mode. you can't change permission mode mid-session. `--input-format stream-json` for warm subprocesses has open bugs
the sdk's `canUseTool` callback is the single hook that solves most of these. it fires for AskUserQuestion so you can render clarifying questions as discord buttons, it handles tool approval per-call so the bot decides at runtime what to allow, and it's fail-closed (callback error = tool denied, vs cli hooks which are fail-open). you also get typed message objects, session resume/fork as `query()` options, and `setPermissionMode()` mid-session
performance is comparable, i benchmarked both on sprite hardware and got ~2-8s sdk vs ~3-6s cli. sessions are the same jsonl files on disk so you can ssh into a sprite and `claude --resume` a conversation that started through the sdk. no lock-in either way

we're building this. i guess Andrej gave a good reason to release this early
Quoting @karpathy
The next step for autoresearch is that it has to be asynchronously massively collaborative for agents (think: SETI@home style). The goal is not to emulate a single PhD student, it's to emulate a research community of them.
Current code synchronously grows a single thread of commits in a particular research direction. But the original repo is more of a seed, from which could sprout commits contributed by agents on all kinds of different research directions or for different compute platforms. Git(Hub) is *almost* but not really suited for this. It has a softly built in assumption of one "master" branch, which temporarily forks off into PRs just to merge back a bit later.
I tried to prototype something super lightweight that could have a flavor of this, e.g. just a Discussion, written by my agent as a summary of its overnight run:
Alternatively, a PR has the benefit of exact commits:
but you'd never want to actually merge it... You'd just want to "adopt" and accumulate branches of commits. But even in this lightweight way, you could ask your agent to first read the Discussions/PRs using GitHub CLI for inspiration, and after its research is done, contribute a little "paper" of findings back.
I'm not actually exactly sure what this should look like, but it's a big idea that is more general than just the autoresearch repo specifically. Agents can in principle easily juggle and collaborate on thousands of commits across arbitrary branch structures. Existing abstractions will accumulate stress as intelligence, attention and tenacity cease to be bottlenecks.

summary:
this usually happens because of some combination of these, roughly in order of importance:
1. slopping without a system design direction in mind, e.g. DDD
2. slopping without a coding style in mind, e.g. functional, oop, tdd, etc
3. slopping without quality gates, pre-commit hooks, pre-pull hooks, etc
if you are doing all of that and codex still makes massively additive prs, like 900 additions and 100 deletions, it is usually because it is trying to keep everything backward compatible. whether that is good or bad is subjective and highly contextual
if in step 1 you explicitly tell it to never preserve backward compatibility, then the problem may be in how your codebase is designed. for example, tdd and no backward compatibility can contradict each other, because tdd often means creating tests that lock features or changes in place. codex is dumb, so it does not realize it needs to delete stale tests
so codex reads "no backward compatibility," then sees tests that lock the feature in place, and because it is biased to remove as little as possible (primed to minimize rm), it still ends up being additive
the way i think about solving this is giving in to the clanker a bit during execution, then doing deliberate sweeps periodically. you can automate that if you want (with `codex exec` in ci)
this is also the kind of problem that slowly solves itself with every +0.1v of codex. i have already noticed that gpt-4.5 xhigh is much more proactive about cleaning up stale tests after itself.
one thing that could help is adding some clarification about this tension in AGENTS.md
hooks can solve this too, like a session-end hook that forces the clanker to do a sweep of stale tests (codex has this now)
Quoting @xeophon
requesting a "with how few lines and small changes can you solve this swe-bench problem" eval so openai can hill climb the shit out of it

having just watched the recent @yacinelearning podcast with @tensorqt and @thelokasiffers, i've thought more about this, and i'm actually optimistic about @paradigmainc's flywheel largely mitigating this inherent bias in modern scientific literature.
when u look at a flywheel graph, what u see isn't a post-hoc rationalization of scientific findings heavily polished for public appeal and reviewer satisfaction, but an honest representation of the scientific process in its truest form, exposing both the original inspirations and the abandoned deadends. the presentation is not longer constrained to whatever story the authors decide to tell. the story can be extracted from the graph, but the graph is there for everyone to transparently scrutinize and explore.
besides the transparency, the automated research features allow one to point resources at an idea, and have them stretch and manipulate it in all sorts of directions, to reveal its true shape and limitations and document them properly.
why didn't this idea pan out? what observation actually led to this hypothesis? what deadends were abondoned along the way? what branches were left unexplored? the answers to all these questions are made explicit in the directed graph flywheel conveniently exposes.
Quoting @leothecurious
there's probably a nontrivial amount of valuable research time that has been wasted over the years as a direct consequence of the notorious positivity bias of scientific literature. in my own r&d work, i've spent considerable time trying to figure out exactly why methods from seemingly interesting papers have failed upon contact with reality. almost every paper i come across spends tens of pages describing exactly what their method gets right relative to prior work, and if u're lucky, it'll includes a few vague lines about the limitations towards the paper's conclusion. understanding the root causes of the failure modes and fundamental limitations is typically one of the most informative parts of any engineering workflow. whereas the successes of a method help identify its general position relative to others, its unique failures can expose the precise shape of it, often in a way that informs future improvements or exposes explicit trade-offs. if we put human ego aside, one can build a highly productive research career out of the simple habit of taking exciting but nascent ideas, stretching them out in a hundred ways, and then describing the failures in great detail. alas, an idea is a scientist's child, and rarely is a parent ready to expose every flaw in their own for the whole world to witness.

clean_summary:
Browserbase? The firecrawl browser? Many are sleeping on Vercel’s agent browser, which is completely free. It allows interaction with UI elements like clicking, typing, filling forms, selecting options, dragging and dropping, and uploading files. It can capture artifacts such as screenshots, PDFs, WebM videos, traces, and DevTools profiles. Users can reuse Chrome login or profile state via --profile or AGENT_BROWSER_PROFILE, or attach to an existing Chrome session through CDP. It can read page state, run JavaScript, and manage browser state including tabs, cookies, storage, and geolocation. It also supports opening, navigating, and inspecting pages with accessibility snapshots, as well as inspecting, recording, or mocking network activity, including HAR logs.

To get started, install with 'brew install agent-browser' and add the skill with 'npx skills add --skill agent-browser'. The tool is documented on GitHub at vercel-labs/agent-browser.

summary:
i've been doing a lot of frontend work with codex recently, so after banging my head against it for a while, here are some tips
- keep iterations small. asking for a full one-shot redesign will create breaking changes
- when functional or visual regressions happen, ask codex to check the diffs (pre regression). once fixed, ask it to add a few small, tasteful tests to stop those regressions from resurfacing. that way, the next time something breaks, it can catch it through the tests without having to visually inspect the frontend
- work ddd. this is the most effective one. codex is not (yet) very good at seeing its frontend work, so domain-driven design keeps the codebase organized in an almost visual way. that means codex will know where to look when you mention specific visual items in your frontend. for example, if you say “the confirm button in the delete-project modal should turn red on hover”, codex has a much better chance of finding it in something like `/projects/delete-project-modal/confirm-button/` instead of guessing its way through a pile of generic components
- use something like agent-browser or dev-browser to let codex visually inspect changes, or reproduce issues before and after bug fixes.
- have some kind of north star principles for codex. for example, if you are refactoring from framework x to framework y, make sure to remind codex that you do not want to reintroduce framework x after the refactor. if things should stay visually or functionally equivalent, the features should be reimplemented in a framework y native way, with no weird hacks or workarounds
- use mock service worker (MSW) to let your clanker work and iterate locally faster without depending on a real db or api
what does not seem to work yet:
- sending videos for codex to review complex actions or interaction bugs

clean_title: Overworking isn't the key to success or well-being
summary:
nerds are always overcomplicating things. overwork isn't measured by hours worked, it's measured by the downstream impact those hours have on your relationships and self care. you can put in an insane number of hours and still maintain healthy relationships with your partner, family, and friends, plus a solid self care baseline. if you can't maintain those outcomes while working more than 8 hours a day, that's either a skill issue, or you're just looking for excuses to be a lazy ass hedonist who would rather rot on a beach drinking martinis until he dies than contribute to the progress and benefit of humanity
Quoting @dhh
You can’t outwork the whole world. There’s always going to be someone somewhere willing to work as hard as you. Someone just as hungry. Or hungrier.
Assuming you can work harder and longer than someone else is giving yourself too much credit for your effort and not enough for theirs. Putting in 1,001 hours to someone else’s 1,000 isn’t going to tip the scale in your favor.
What’s worse is when management holds up certain people as having a great “work ethic” because they’re always around, always available, always working. That’s a terrible example of a work ethic and a great example of someone who’s overworked.
A great work ethic isn’t about working whenever you’re called upon. It’s about doing what you say you’re going to do, putting in a fair day’s work, respecting the work, respecting the customer, respecting coworkers, not wasting time, not creating unnecessary work for other people, and not being a bottleneck. Work ethic is about being a fundamentally good person that others can count on and enjoy working with.
So how do people get ahead if it’s not about outworking everyone else?
People make it because they’re talented, they’re lucky, they’re in the right place at the right time, they know how to work with other people, they know how to sell an idea, they know what moves people, they can tell a story, they know which details matter and which don’t, they can see the big and small pictures in every situation, and they know how to do something with an opportunity. And for so many other reasons.
So get the outwork myth out of your head. Stop equating work ethic with excessive work hours. Neither is going to get you ahead or help you find calm.
[The Outwork Myth — It Doesn't Have To Be Crazy At Work, 2018]
clean_summary: Overwork isn't measured by hours but by its impact on relationships and self-care. You can work many hours and still maintain healthy connections and a baseline of self-care, but if you can't do so while working more than eight hours a day, it's either a skill issue or you're making excuses to avoid contributing meaningfully. The idea that you can outwork everyone else is a myth; success depends on talent, luck, timing, collaboration, storytelling, and recognizing what matters. A strong work ethic involves reliability, respect, efficiency, and being a good person others can depend on, not just working long hours.

clean_title: The redundancy of `/loop` over `/goal` in AI workflows
summary:
`/loops` are an unnecessary abstraction over `/goals`, created to force a buzzword into existence
a `/loop` is effectively the same thing as a `/goal`, because the model can create its own stopping condition and decide when to stop. at least in most implementations
a `/goal` can achieve the same result as a `/loop` if the stopping condition is open-ended. i do this all the time with `/goal`
in theory:
`/loop find dead code and delete it`
should be better than:
`/goal find dead code and delete it`
because `/goal` would more or less require finding all the dead code first in order to precisely define the “all” stopping condition , while `/loop` can stay open ended and keep searching for dead code
the problem is that:
1. as i said, `/goal` can already do this with an open-ended stopping condition
2. `/loop` can still give itself a stopping condition anyway and decide to stop at any time
so in practice, `/loop` doesn’t really add anything meaningful. it is just `/goal` for retards
clean_summary: The tweet argues that `/loops` are an unnecessary abstraction over `/goals`, since both can achieve similar results. A `/loop` is essentially the same as a `/goal` because the model can set its own stopping condition and decide when to stop. In practice, `/loop` doesn't add any meaningful functionality because `/goal` can also have an open-ended stopping condition, and `/loop` can set a stop at any time. The tweet suggests that `/loop` is just a rebranding of `/goal` with no real benefit.
